sections.skill: Spot information that may be out of date

questions.prompt: Which fact is most likely to change over time?

choices.text: The spelling of "elephant"
The number of days in a week
A museum's ticket price
The boiling point of water

questions.correct_answer: A museum's ticket price
questions.intro: Information can be OUTDATED even when it was once true. A model's built-in knowledge stops at its training cutoff, and sources it retrieves may also be old. Facts that change often include prices, laws and rules, schedules and opening hours, who holds an office, software features, and records such as "the tallest building." Clues that an answer may be stale: no date given, words like "currently" or "latest" without a date, or a source more than a year or two old for a fast-changing topic. To check, find a CURRENT, DATED source, ideally the organization that controls the fact.

sections.skill: Compare stale information with an old milk carton

questions.prompt: Why does a milk carton have a date?

choices.text: To set the price
Fresh milk can go bad over time
To show where it was made
To look nice

questions.correct_answer: Fresh milk can go bad over time
questions.intro: A milk carton has a date because milk that was fresh last month may not be good today. Information works the same way. A store's hours, a ticket price or a rule might have been right when it was written but wrong now. Some information keeps for a long time, like the number of legs on a spider. Other information "spoils" quickly, like prices and schedules. Before using information that spoils quickly, check its date, the way you would check the date on milk.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Handle source dates and conflicts carefully

questions.prompt: A page says "last updated this week," but its prices mention an event from three years ago. What should you think?

choices.text: The page must be fake
The event must be happening now
The edit may be minor; the prices may be old
Everything on the page must be current now

questions.correct_answer: The edit may be minor; the prices may be old
questions.intro: Dates on sources need care too. A web page may show "last updated" for a minor edit while its main content is old, or a news article may describe a plan that later changed. When you find two sources that disagree, prefer the more recent one from the organization in charge, and check whether something changed between their dates. For decisions with deadlines, such as applications, travel or taxes, confirm the facts close to the date you act, because they can change even after you checked.
questions.feedback: An update date does not prove all content is current.
